16710:
Something is unintentional when it happens without the person meaning or planning for it to happen. In other words, the person did not do it on purpose. It was an accident, a slip, or simply something that occurred without any desire or decision behind it.

Think of it this way: when you intend to do something, you make a conscious choice in your mind — you think "I want this to happen" and then you act. When something is unintentional, that mental step of choosing never happened. The result came about without anyone willing it into existence.
Breaking the Word Down

The word is built from two parts. "Intentional" means done with intention — on purpose, deliberately, with a goal in mind. The prefix "un-" simply flips that meaning to its opposite. So "unintentional" literally means without intention.
What It Describes

As an adjective, "unintentional" always describes a noun — usually an action, an event, a mistake, a consequence, or a result. It tells you the nature of that thing: that it was not planned or meant.

Here are some natural examples:

  • "His rude comment was completely unintentional — he didn't realize how it sounded."
  • "The unintentional spill ruined her notebook."
  • "It was an unintentional error in the report."
  • "The movie's unintentional humor made the audience laugh despite its serious tone."
  • "She caused unintentional harm by sharing information she didn't know was private."

Notice that in every case, the noun being described (comment, spill, error, humor, harm) is something that happened without the person consciously choosing it to happen.
The Key Contrast: Intentional vs. Unintentional

The clearest way to understand this word is to hold it next to its opposite.

An intentional act is one where the person thought about it and decided to do it. A thief who plans a robbery and carries it out — that is intentional. A chess player who sacrifices a piece to win the game — intentional. A writer who chooses a specific word for effect — intentional.

An unintentional act is one where no such thinking or deciding took place. You accidentally knock a glass off a table — unintentional. You hurt a friend's feelings with a joke you thought was harmless — unintentional. A scientist discovers something while looking for something completely different — an unintentional discovery. A driver runs a red light because they were distracted — unintentional.

The deciding factor is always the same: Was there a conscious plan or desire behind it? If yes → intentional. If no → unintentional.
Degrees of "Unintentional"

Not all unintentional things happen the same way. They can fall into a few different situations:

Pure accident — The person had no part in causing it beyond being present. A bird flies into your windshield. Completely unintentional.

Carelessness without bad intent — The person did something that led to a result they didn't want. Texting while walking and bumping into someone. Unintentional, but perhaps avoidable.

Ignorance — The person did something without knowing it would cause a certain outcome. Giving someone a food they're allergic to because you didn't know about their allergy — the harm caused is unintentional.

Side effects — A main action is chosen, but an additional result tags along unexpectedly. A doctor prescribes medicine and it causes unintentional drowsiness. The medicine was intentional; the drowsiness was not.

In all these cases, the word "unintentional" accurately applies, because the specific outcome was never part of anyone's plan.
An Important Nuance: Unintentional Does Not Always Mean Excused

People sometimes assume that if something is unintentional, it carries no responsibility. That is not always true, and the word itself does not make that claim. "Unintentional" only tells you about the presence or absence of intent — it says nothing about whether the person should have been more careful, or whether the harm caused still needs to be fixed.

For example, an unintentional car accident caused by a driver who was texting is still legally and morally significant, even though the crash wasn't meant to happen. The word describes how it happened, not whether it matters.
The Adverb Form: Unintentionally

When you want to describe how an action was done rather than describe a noun, you use the adverb form: unintentionally.

  • "She unintentionally interrupted him mid-sentence."
  • "He unintentionally became the leader of the group."
  • "The policy unintentionally discouraged new applicants."

Here, "unintentionally" is modifying a verb — it tells you in what manner the action took place. Same meaning, just a different grammatical role.
Synonyms (Words With Similar Meaning)

Knowing related words helps you understand the full picture:

Accidental — Perhaps the most common synonym. "It was accidental" and "It was unintentional" are almost identical in meaning, though "unintentional" puts a stronger emphasis on the absence of intent, while "accidental" puts more emphasis on the random or chance nature of the event.

Inadvertent — Means happening without proper attention or awareness. Slightly more formal. An inadvertent mistake is one made without noticing.

Unwitting — Means done without knowledge or awareness. Often used when someone causes something without realizing they are doing so. "An unwitting accomplice" is someone who helped without knowing they were helping.

Involuntary — Means done without conscious control. This is slightly different — it often refers to bodily reactions (an involuntary flinch) or actions made under pressure, rather than simple accidents.

Unplanned — Means not arranged or decided in advance. Close to unintentional but focuses more on the absence of a plan rather than the absence of desire.
Antonyms (Words With the Opposite Meaning)

Intentional — Done on purpose, with full awareness and will.

Deliberate — Done with careful thought and full intention. Often implies the person thought it through before acting.

Calculated — Done with specific goals in mind, often implying a level of strategy or even coldness.

Premeditated — Planned in advance. This word is especially used in legal and serious contexts (e.g., premeditated crime).

Willful — Done by choice, often implying the person knew it might cause harm but did it anyway.
Common Collocations (Words You'll Often See Paired With "Unintentional")

Some nouns naturally appear beside "unintentional" in everyday English:

  • Unintentional mistake / error — a very common pairing
  • Unintentional harm / damage / injury — used in law, medicine, ethics
  • Unintentional consequence / result / effect — used in policy, science, analysis
  • Unintentional humor / comedy — when something is funny without meaning to be
  • Unintentional insult / offense — when someone upsets another person without meaning to
  • Unintentional bias — a prejudice someone holds without being aware of it
A Final Summary

Unintentional is an adjective meaning not done on purpose; happening without a plan, desire, or conscious choice. It describes actions, events, mistakes, effects, or results that occurred without anyone willing them to happen. It is the opposite of intentional, deliberate, or planned. The word makes no judgment about whether the outcome matters or whether someone is responsible — it only tells you that the intent to cause that specific outcome was absent.

Whenever you see or hear "unintentional," ask yourself one simple question: Did the person mean for this to happen? If the answer is no — that is exactly what the word is telling you.
16711:
Uninterested means having no interest in something or someone — you simply do not care about it, you feel no curiosity toward it, and you have no desire to pay attention to it.

When you are uninterested in something, it is not that you hate it or are against it. You just feel nothing toward it. It doesn't pull your attention. It doesn't make you curious. It doesn't make you want to engage. It is as if that thing doesn't exist for you emotionally.

Think of it like a dial that goes from "very interested" to "completely uninterested." When the dial is at zero — no spark, no engagement, no care — that is the state of being uninterested.
What It Feels Like in Real Life

Imagine someone is talking to you about a topic you find deeply boring — say, the detailed history of paperclips. You're not angry about it. You don't hate paperclips. But you have zero desire to listen, learn, or engage. Your mind wanders. Your eyes glaze over. You might nod politely, but inside, you feel nothing. That is what it means to be uninterested.
How to Use It in a Sentence

"Uninterested" is almost always followed by "in" when you specify what the person has no interest in.

  • He was uninterested in money or fame.
  • The students seemed uninterested in the lesson.
  • She appeared uninterested in making new friends.

You can also use it without "in" when the context is already clear:

  • He listened, but his expression was completely uninterested.
  • The dog sniffed the new toy and walked away, uninterested.

You can strengthen it with adverbs like completely, totally, utterly, seemingly, largely, entirely:

  • She was utterly uninterested in the conversation.
  • He was largely uninterested in sports.

• A child forced to sit through an adult conversation about taxes is likely uninterested — they don't hate taxes, they just have no reason to care.
  • An artist who never reads the news is uninterested in current events — it's not hostility, just a complete absence of curiosity.
  • Someone scrolling through their phone while a friend speaks is behaving in an uninterested way.
  • "The hiring manager seemed uninterested in my qualifications and kept looking at her watch."
The Most Important Distinction You Must Know

The single biggest source of confusion with this word is mixing it up with "disinterested." These two words are not the same, even though many people mistakenly use them interchangeably.

Here is the clear difference:

Uninterested = You don't care. You have no curiosity or engagement.
Disinterested = You have no personal stake, bias, or selfish motive in something. You are neutral and impartial.

A judge in a court case should be disinterested — they have no personal investment in either side winning. But they should not be uninterested — they absolutely should care about the truth and justice.

A good referee in a football match should be disinterested (they don't favor either team), but they must not be uninterested (they need to pay close attention to every play).

Think of it this way:

  • Disinterested is about fairness — "I have no skin in the game."
  • Uninterested is about caring — "I don't care about this at all."

If someone asks you to make a decision and you say "I'm disinterested," you're saying you're unbiased. If you say "I'm uninterested," you're saying you don't want to be involved at all.
Synonyms (Words That Mean the Same or Similar)

These words all carry the core flavor of "uninterested," though each has a slight shade of difference:

  • Indifferent — You feel neither positive nor negative; you simply don't care. This is the closest synonym.
  • Apathetic — Similar to indifferent, but often implies a deeper, more heavy lack of motivation or energy to engage.
  • Incurious — Specifically lacking curiosity; no desire to learn or find out.
  • Detached — Emotionally uninvolved or removed from something.
  • Disengaged — Not actively participating or paying attention.
  • Unconcerned — You don't feel worried about or invested in something.
  • Bored — A more casual, everyday word meaning something fails to hold your attention.

• Interested — You feel drawn to something; you want to know more.
  • Curious — You have a desire to explore and learn.
  • Engaged — You are actively paying attention and participating.
  • Enthusiastic — You feel excited and eager.
  • Invested — You care about the outcome.
  • Attentive — You are focused and paying close attention.

1. It describes a state, not an action.
Being uninterested is something you feel, not something you do. You don't "do" uninterested — you are uninterested. It's a condition of your attention and emotions at a given moment.

2. It is not the same as disliking something.
If you dislike something, you have an active negative reaction to it. "Uninterested" is more passive than that — you have no reaction at all. For example, you can be uninterested in chess without disliking chess.

3. It can be temporary or permanent.
You can be uninterested in a topic right now (temporary — maybe you're tired), or you can be someone who is generally uninterested in a subject for life (permanent — it's just not your thing).

4. It applies to people, topics, activities, and ideas.
You can be uninterested in a person (no desire to get to know them), a topic (history, football, fashion), an activity (hiking, cooking), or an idea (a business proposal, a plan).

Uninterested = completely lacking interest in something or someone. No curiosity. No engagement. No care. The opposite of being drawn to something.

The one thing to never forget: uninterested ≠ disinterested. Uninterested is about caring. Disinterested is about bias. Getting this right immediately marks you as someone who uses English with precision.
16712: Uninterrupted means continuing from beginning to end with nothing getting in the way — no breaks, no pauses, no stops, no disturbances of any kind.
The Simple Idea Behind the Word

Think of a river flowing smoothly. No rocks blocking it, no dam stopping it — just water moving freely from one point to another. That flow is uninterrupted. Now take that same idea and apply it to almost anything in life — sleep, work, a conversation, a view — and you have the essence of what "uninterrupted" means.

Something is uninterrupted when it started, ran its full course, and nothing came in the way before it was naturally supposed to end.
The Two Main Ways It Is Used

For activities, events, and stretches of time — this is the most common use. When an activity or a period of time is uninterrupted, it means nothing broke it or paused it midway.

"She had six hours of uninterrupted sleep" means she slept for six hours straight — no alarm, no noise, no child crying, nothing woke her up in between. "I need two hours of uninterrupted work" means two hours where nobody calls, knocks on the door, or sends messages to pull attention away. "The concert was an uninterrupted two-hour performance" means no intermissions, no technical failures, no pauses — just two solid hours of music.

Notice a pattern in all these examples: there is always a sense that the thing could have been interrupted — but it wasn't. That's a quiet but important part of the word's meaning.

For physical space, views, and signals — "uninterrupted" is also used to describe a physical path, a line of sight, or a signal that stretches from one point to another with no obstacles blocking it.

"From the hilltop, we had an uninterrupted view of the ocean" means nothing — no trees, no buildings, no hills — stood between the viewer and the ocean. "The highway offered an uninterrupted stretch of road for over 200 miles" means the road went on without a single traffic light, stop sign, or crossing for 200 miles. "The radio tower provides uninterrupted coverage across the region" means the signal reaches everywhere without dropping or cutting out.

To fully understand "uninterrupted," it helps to clearly understand what an interruption is. An interruption is anything that breaks the flow or continuity of something — a pause, a stop, a disturbance, or an obstacle. A phone ringing during a meeting interrupts the meeting. A power cut during a movie interrupts the movie. A wall blocking your view interrupts your line of sight. Remove all of those things, and what you have left is something uninterrupted.
This Word Sets a High Bar

"Uninterrupted" is an absolute-leaning word. It does not mean "mostly without interruptions" or "rarely broken." It means genuinely without any interruption at all. Even one break technically disqualifies it.

If someone slept for eight hours but woke up once at 3 AM, their sleep was not uninterrupted — even though most of it was smooth. If a road stretches for 100 miles but has one traffic light somewhere in the middle, it is not an uninterrupted stretch. The word demands a clean, complete, zero-interruptions standard.

"Uninterrupted" carries a quiet sense of completeness, smoothness, and wholeness. It suggests that something had the full space it needed — nothing crowded in, nothing cut it short, nothing broke its rhythm. This is why the word is so often used for things we value deeply, like deep sleep, focused work, a meaningful conversation, or a breathtaking view. It implies ideal conditions.

Knowing similar words sharpens your understanding of this one.

Continuous is very close in meaning but more neutral — it simply states that something kept going. "Uninterrupted" goes further by emphasizing that nothing came in the way to stop it. Unbroken focuses on something being whole and intact, without gaps. Undisturbed leans more toward the absence of noise or disturbance in a peaceful sense, while "uninterrupted" focuses on the absence of breaks in flow or activity. Sustained implies something was actively kept going over time, whereas "uninterrupted" is more neutral about whether effort was involved. Seamless describes a process or transition that is smooth with no visible joins.

The clearest opposite is simply interrupted — something that was broken or stopped midway. Other related opposites include disrupted (thrown into disorder, often suddenly), broken (having gaps or pauses, not continuous), fragmented (split into pieces, not whole), and sporadic (happening at irregular intervals with gaps in between).
Common Phrases and Contexts Where You Will See This Word

You will encounter "uninterrupted" most often in these combinations: uninterrupted sleep (sleep that isn't broken by waking up), uninterrupted time or hours (a stretch of time completely free from disturbances), uninterrupted power supply — often abbreviated as UPS (a device that keeps electricity flowing even when the main power cuts out), uninterrupted view (a view with no obstacles), uninterrupted access (the ability to use or reach something at any point without being blocked), uninterrupted service (like internet or water supply that works without cutting out), and uninterrupted focus or concentration (working or thinking without being pulled away).
A Simple Test to Remember the Word

Whenever you come across "uninterrupted," ask yourself one question: Did this thing run its full course with absolutely nothing getting in the way? If the answer is yes — it was uninterrupted. If even one thing broke it, paused it, or got in the way — it was not.
16713:
Union means the joining of two or more things into one, or the state of being joined together. It captures the idea that separate things have come together to form something combined — and that the result is now, in some meaningful sense, a single whole.

Think of it this way: if you take two rivers and they flow into each other, the point where they meet and begin moving as one stream is a union. The two became one.

This idea of coming together as one is the thread that runs through every use of this word, no matter the context.
1. General Use — Things or People Joining Together

In its broadest sense, a union is simply the act or result of joining things together.

  • The union of two companies (a merger)
  • The union of flavors in a dish
  • The union of ideas from two different thinkers into a single theory

You can use it whenever two or more things combine into a cohesive whole. The focus is always on the joining itself, and on the resulting oneness.

One of the most common uses of "union" is for a group of states, countries, or territories that have formally joined together under a shared system of governance or agreement.

Examples:

  • The United States — originally thirteen separate colonies, they formed a union. The word "union" in American history refers specifically to the federal government holding all the states together as one nation (this is why during the Civil War, the Northern side was called "the Union" — they were fighting to keep the states joined).
  • The European Union (EU) — a political and economic union of European countries that have agreed to share certain laws, a common market, and (for many members) a common currency.
  • The Soviet Union (USSR) — a now-dissolved union of Soviet republics under one communist government.

What makes something a union rather than just a group of countries is the idea of formal, structural joining — they've given up some independence to function together as a combined entity.

A labor union (also called a trade union, especially in British English) is an organized association of workers in a particular trade, industry, or company, formed to protect and promote their collective interests.

Here's the logic: a single worker has very little power when dealing with a large employer. But if thousands of workers join together — forming a union — they can negotiate as a group. This is called collective bargaining. They negotiate together for better wages, safer working conditions, fair hours, and protection against unfair treatment.

A labor union is a union in the most human sense: individual people who, by joining together, become stronger than they would be alone.

Examples: a teachers' union, a miners' union, a nurses' union.

The head of a union is usually called a union leader or union president. Members pay union dues (fees) to fund the organization.
4. Union as a Personal Bond — Marriage and Partnerships

"Union" is used in a formal, often dignified way to refer to the joining of two people in marriage or a committed partnership.

  • "Their union was celebrated by family and friends." (meaning: their marriage)
  • A civil union is a legally recognized relationship between two people, similar to marriage but sometimes distinct from it in legal status (the specifics vary by country and jurisdiction).

This use carries a sense of formality and permanence. It emphasizes that the two people are now, in a real sense, joined as one — legally, socially, and personally.

In mathematics, specifically in set theory, a union has a precise, technical meaning:

The union of two (or more) sets is a new set that contains every element that belongs to any of those sets — without repetition.

For example:

  • Set A = {1, 2, 3}
  • Set B = {3, 4, 5}
  • The union of A and B = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}

Notice that 3 appears in both sets, but in the union, it appears only once. The union collects everything, but doesn't duplicate.

The symbol for union is ∪, and you'd write this as A ∪ B.

The underlying idea is still the same: you are bringing two things together into one combined collection.

In a more technical, specialized context, a union can refer to a type of pipe fitting used to connect two sections of pipe.

A union fitting is designed so that the connection can easily be tightened or loosened without having to rotate the entire pipe. It's a small but essential component in plumbing and mechanical systems.

This is a less common use in everyday language, but worth knowing — it comes directly from the core meaning: a device that joins things together.

In the context of textiles, a union (also called union cloth or union fabric) refers to a fabric woven from two different types of fiber — for example, a blend of cotton and linen, or cotton and wool.

The name reflects the fact that two different materials have been united into one fabric. This is a specialized, old-fashioned use that you're unlikely to encounter in modern everyday conversation, but it exists.

Beyond just the dictionary definitions, "union" carries a certain feeling with it. It tends to suggest:

  • Strength through togetherness — things joined are stronger than things apart
  • Formality and permanence — a union isn't a casual grouping; it implies a real, lasting bond
  • Shared purpose — the things or people in a union are oriented toward something together

This is why the word feels weighty and meaningful. When someone says "union," they're not just describing proximity or association — they're describing a real joining, a true combination.

ContextWhat "union" means
GeneralThe act or result of joining things into one
PoliticalA group of states/countries formally joined under shared governance
LaborAn organized group of workers acting collectively to protect their rights
PersonalA marriage or formal partnership between people
MathematicsA set containing all elements of two or more sets combined
PlumbingA fitting that connects two pipe sections
TextilesA fabric blended from two different fiber types

The word "union" is remarkably consistent across all these uses. Whether it's countries, workers, people, rivers, or numbers — a union is always about separate things choosing or being brought to come together, and the wholeness that results from that joining.
16714:
Unique means one of a kind — there is exactly one of something, and nothing else in existence is exactly like it.

Think of it this way: if you have something unique, you could search the entire world (or universe, or whichever context applies) and you would never find another thing that is exactly the same. There is simply no duplicate. No copy. No equivalent.

"Every person's fingerprints are unique."
→ No two people on Earth have the exact same fingerprint pattern. Each one exists only once.

"The original Mona Lisa is unique."
→ There is only one original painting. Everything else is a copy or reproduction.

This is the most important thing to understand about this word, and it's something many people get wrong.

Unique is not a matter of degree. Something either is unique (one of a kind) or it is not unique (meaning at least one other similar thing exists). There is no in-between.

This means that, strictly and correctly speaking, you cannot say:

  • "very unique"
  • "quite unique"
  • "somewhat unique"
  • "fairly unique"
  • "almost unique"
  • "more unique than"

Why? Because if something is unique, it already means it's the only one — the absolute maximum. Saying "very unique" is like saying "very one-of-a-kind." The word "very" adds nothing, because there's no scale here. Either there is one, or there isn't.

The right way: Just say "unique" on its own, without modifiers.

✅ "Her voice is unique."
❌ "Her voice is very unique."
Common Informal Usage (And Why It's Technically Imprecise)

In everyday conversation, people very commonly use "unique" to simply mean unusual, distinctive, or remarkable — not necessarily "one of a kind" in the strictest sense.

"That's a unique design." → (Meaning: That's an unusual / distinctive design.)

"He has a unique personality." → (Meaning: He has a very unusual or striking personality.)

This loose usage is everywhere — in advertisements, casual speech, journalism — and people understand what is meant. However, it is not the precise, technically correct meaning of the word. When you use "unique" to mean merely "unusual," you are watering down its true power. The word loses its sharpness.

A good writer or precise speaker reserves "unique" for its true meaning: genuinely one of a kind.

"Unique" is very commonly followed by the word "to", meaning something exists only within a specific place, group, time period, or context.

"This species of bird is unique to the Amazon rainforest."
→ This bird exists nowhere else on Earth. Only the Amazon has it.

"This problem is not unique to our company."
→ Other companies face this problem too; it's not exclusively ours.

"Each era in history is unique to its time."
→ Each period belongs to its own time and cannot be replicated.

The phrase "unique to" is a very precise and useful way to say: found only here, and nowhere else.

It's easy to confuse "unique" with words like rare, special, unusual, or distinctive. Here's the difference:

  • Rare means something exists, but not very often — there are still multiple examples of it, just few. A rare diamond is hard to find, but there are other rare diamonds. A unique diamond would mean there is only one such diamond in existence.
  • Special means something is treated or regarded with extra care or distinction. It doesn't necessarily mean one of a kind.
  • Unusual means something that doesn't happen often or doesn't follow the normal pattern. Many unusual things can exist.
  • Distinctive means something has clear features that set it apart and make it recognizable. But it doesn't have to be the only one of its kind.

Unique is stronger than all of these. It is the ultimate claim: there is no other.
Summary of All the Key Points

1. Core meaning: One of a kind. Nothing else exactly like it exists.
  2. It's absolute: Don't say "very unique," "quite unique," or "almost unique." These are technically wrong because unique has no degrees — it already means the maximum.
  3. "Unique to": Means found only in a particular context, place, or group.
  4. Loose informal use: People often use it to mean just "unusual" or "distinctive." This is widespread but imprecise.
  5. Stronger than: rare, special, unusual, distinctive — because it means the only one, not just uncommon or noteworthy.
A Few Final Examples to Cement It

"Each human being is unique." — No two humans are exactly alike in every way.

"The dinosaur fossil they discovered was unique — no other specimen like it had ever been found." — One of a kind.

"This custom is unique to this small village." — Only this village practices it; no one else does.

"The situation we're in is unique." — Nothing like this has ever happened before; there's no precedent.

The power of "unique" lies in its absoluteness. When you use it correctly, it makes a bold and total claim — this is the only one of its kind. That's what gives the word its weight.
16715: The heart of this word is simple: sameness happening at the same time. When multiple people, voices, or things do the exact same thing at the exact same moment, that is unison. It captures perfect togetherness — not just being close or similar, but being identical and simultaneous.

In music, unison has a precise definition. It describes the situation where two or more voices or instruments are singing or playing the exact same note at the exact same time. Not different notes that blend pleasantly together (that is called harmony) — but literally, the same note.

Imagine ten people in a choir all singing the note C at the same moment. They are singing in unison. If instead each singer picks a different note that fits nicely with the others, that is harmony. Harmony is beautiful difference working together. Unison is perfect sameness happening together.

One accurate nuance worth knowing: true unison technically means the same pitch, at the same octave. In real-world choral or band performance, a bass and a soprano might follow the same melody but sing it an octave apart because of the natural ranges of their voices. Strictly speaking, that is not pure unison — but in everyday musical language, people still commonly call it "singing in unison," meaning they are all on the same melody rather than split into separate harmony parts. The key takeaway is: unison means same note, same moment. The octave subtlety is something to be aware of but not worry about as a learner.

Outside of music, unison describes any situation where people or things act, move, or speak simultaneously and identically — as if they were a single thing.

The soldiers marched in unison — every soldier took every step at exactly the same moment. The students answered in unison — everyone said the same thing at the same time. The crowd cheered in unison — thousands of voices rising as one.

Notice that two conditions must both be met. If people do the same thing but at different times, that is not unison. If they act at the same time but do different things, that is also not unison. Unison requires both sameness and simultaneity.
Its Meaning in Thought and Opinion

Unison can also describe a state where people are in complete agreement — thinking, feeling, or deciding the same thing. "The board spoke in unison about the need for change." Here, they did not necessarily all speak at the same instant; rather, their views were perfectly aligned, as if coming from one mind. This is the most figurative use of the word, but it follows the same core logic: multiple parties merging into sameness.

You will almost always see this word used as part of the phrase in unison rather than as a standalone noun. This phrase describes how something is done — together, as one, simultaneously. While you can say "there was perfect unison in their performance," it is far more natural and common to say "they performed in unison."
How Unison Differs from Similar Words

Harmony implies that different elements blend together — there is variety working as a team. Unison implies no variety at all — everyone is doing or singing the exact same thing.

Agreement is a broad, casual word. Unison carries a stronger sense of precision, timing, and completeness.

Synchrony refers to things happening at the same time but does not require them to be identical — two clocks can run in synchrony while displaying different hours across time zones. Unison requires both sameness and simultaneity.

Unison means the exact same thing, expressed by multiple parties, at the same time. Whether in music (the same note), in physical action (the same movement), or in thought (the same view), it always points to perfect, simultaneous sameness. The word carries a feeling of unity and precision — when things happen in unison, there is no gap, no difference, no staggering. Everything lines up exactly, as if many have become one.
16716:
A unitard is a tight, stretchy, one-piece garment that covers your entire torso and your legs — and sometimes your arms too — all in one continuous piece of clothing. Think of it as a single suit that goes from your shoulders (or neck) all the way down to your ankles (or feet), with no break or separation anywhere in between.

The word itself is a clue: uni means "one," and the garment is a single, uninterrupted unit of clothing — no top, no bottom, just one piece.

A unitard hugs the body very closely. It is form-fitting — meaning it follows the shape of your body tightly, like a second skin. It does not have a loose or baggy fit. Because of this, it is almost always made from materials that can stretch easily, such as spandex, Lycra, or nylon blends. These fabrics allow the person wearing it to move freely without the clothing pulling, bunching, or restricting movement.

Unitards come in several variations:

  • Sleeveless — no arms, just the body and legs covered
  • Short-sleeved — covers the upper arm but leaves the forearm bare
  • Long-sleeved — covers the arms all the way to the wrists
  • Footed — the legs continue all the way down and cover the feet
How it is different from similar garments

Since a unitard looks similar to a few other garments, it helps to understand exactly what makes it distinct.

Unitard vs. Leotard:
A leotard is also a tight, one-piece garment — but it only covers your torso, like a swimsuit. Your legs are left bare. A unitard, by contrast, extends downward and covers your legs as well. You can think of a unitard as a leotard with legs attached.

Unitard vs. Bodysuit:
A bodysuit covers the torso and snaps shut at the crotch, but your legs remain bare. A unitard goes further and includes the legs.

Unitard vs. Jumpsuit:
A jumpsuit is also a one-piece garment covering the torso and legs, but it is loose, structured like pants and a top combined, and made from non-stretchy fabric. A unitard is tight, stretchy, and body-hugging — much more like athletic wear.

Unitards are almost always worn for performance or athletic activities where the person needs complete freedom of movement, and where loose clothing would get in the way or look messy.

The most common contexts are:

  • Ballet and dance — Dancers wear unitards because they allow full, unrestricted movement of every part of the body. Choreographers and teachers can also clearly see the dancer's body position, lines, and technique without fabric getting in the way.
  • Gymnastics and acrobatics — Athletes need to bend, flip, and stretch in every direction. A unitard stays in place and never rides up or shifts, which is important for both safety and clean visual presentation during competition.
  • Circus arts — Acrobats and performers wear unitards for the same reasons as gymnasts.
  • Figure skating — Skaters sometimes wear unitards under their costumes or as the costume itself.
  • Theater and stage performance — Performers sometimes wear unitards as a base costume, especially in avant-garde or movement-based productions.
  • Superhero costumes — Many fictional superhero suits (think comic books or films) are visually modeled on the idea of a unitard.
A mental image to lock it in

Imagine you are watching a gymnastics competition on TV. The athlete is wearing a single, shiny, tight-fitting outfit that seamlessly covers her entire body from her shoulders down to her ankles — no visible separation between a "top" and "bottom," no loose fabric anywhere, just one smooth, continuous suit. That is a unitard.

What it isA tight, stretchy, one-piece garment
What it coversTorso + legs (and optionally arms and feet)
Key featureNo separation — one continuous piece
MaterialStretchy fabrics like spandex or Lycra
Who wears itDancers, gymnasts, acrobats, performers
WhyFreedom of movement; stays in place; reveals body lines for performance

That's everything meaningful there is to know about the word unitard as a noun. It's a specific, practical piece of clothing with a clear purpose — and once you've seen one, you'll recognize it instantly.

Unity means the state of being one — or, more precisely, the state in which many things come together to form a single, complete whole. Think of it as the opposite of being broken, divided, or scattered.

If a group of people all pull a rope in the same direction, they are acting as one. That togetherness, that "one-ness," is unity.

Unity is a rich word with several closely related senses. All of them orbit the same central idea — oneness — but applied in different ways.

1. Togetherness and agreement among people

This is the most common everyday use. When people stand together — sharing the same goal, feeling, or purpose — that is unity. It doesn't mean they are all identical or think exactly alike on every matter. It means they are joined by something common and strong enough to hold them together.

Workers went on strike in unity — each one supporting the others.

The nation showed unity in the face of the disaster — people from all regions came together to help.

A key point: unity among people is not the same as everyone being the same. A family with very different personalities can still have unity if they love and support one another. A sports team full of players with different skills can have unity if they work toward the same goal. This is why the phrase "unity in diversity" exists — it captures the idea that oneness can exist within difference, not just despite it.

2. The quality of being a single, coherent whole

This sense of unity is about wholeness and completeness. Something has unity when all its parts fit together smoothly, without contradiction or awkwardness, so that the whole feels like one thing rather than a collection of unrelated pieces.

This applies to creative and intellectual work:

  • A well-written novel has unity — the story, characters, themes, and mood all feel like they belong to the same world and serve the same purpose. Nothing feels out of place.
  • A painting has unity when its colors, shapes, and composition all harmonize — the eye moves through it and senses that every element belongs.
  • A building has unity when its design is consistent throughout.
  • An argument has unity when all its points build toward the same conclusion without drifting off in unrelated directions.

The opposite of this kind of unity is fragmentation — when the parts of something don't hold together and feel disconnected.

3. The number 1 (in mathematics)

In mathematics, unity is a technical term for the number 1. This is a narrower, specialized use. You'll encounter it in expressions like "the square root of unity" (which is 1) or "multiplying by unity" (multiplying by 1, which leaves a value unchanged). Outside of mathematics, this meaning rarely appears.

Understanding what a word doesn't mean is just as important as knowing what it does.

Unity is not uniformity. Uniformity means everything is the same — identical in appearance, behavior, or opinion. Unity simply means being joined together as one. You can have unity among very different people. Uniformity erases differences; unity transcends them.

Unity is not unanimity. Unanimity is when everyone in a group agrees on a specific decision or opinion — a vote where every hand goes up. Unity is broader. A group can have unity (a strong sense of togetherness and shared purpose) even when members disagree on certain things. And a group can reach unanimity on a specific vote without having any real sense of unity at all.

Unity is not forced sameness. Real unity comes from a genuine bond, shared values, or a common goal — not from pressure or coercion. When unity is forced, it's usually not called unity at all; it's called suppression or conformity.
Unity in Different Areas of Life

In politics and society

Governments and leaders speak of national unity when they want citizens to set aside their differences and work together — especially during a crisis, a war, or a period of rebuilding. Political parties speak of party unity when their members agree to support a common policy or candidate. The lack of unity is called division or fragmentation.

In religion and philosophy

Many religious and philosophical traditions use unity to describe the relationship between a person and something greater — God, the universe, or all of existence. Concepts like "unity with the divine" or "the unity of all things" express the idea that beneath all apparent differences, everything is part of one single reality.

In art, writing, and design

As described above, unity is one of the foundational principles of good design and storytelling. It means coherence — the feeling that the whole is more than just the sum of its parts, because the parts belong together.

In everyday speech

You'll hear and read "unity" in many ordinary contexts:

  • "The team's unity was what made them champions."
  • "The speech called for unity during difficult times."
  • "There was a sense of unity among the volunteers."

It's worth noting that unity isn't purely abstract — it's something people feel. When you are in a crowd singing the same song, or when your family comes together after a long time apart, or when teammates celebrate a hard-won victory, there is an unmistakable feeling — a warmth, a sense of belonging, a feeling that you are part of something larger than yourself. That feeling is unity, as it shows up in lived experience.
In a Sentence: The Simplest Summary

Unity is the state in which separate people or things are joined into one — whether through shared purpose, harmony, or a bond strong enough to make them feel and act as a single whole.

Everything else about this word is a variation or application of that idea.

"Unjust" means not fair, not right, or not in line with what people deserve. When something is unjust, it goes against the basic principles of fairness and moral correctness. It describes a situation, action, decision, law, punishment, or treatment that violates what is right and fair.

The simplest way to feel the word: if someone gets hurt, punished, or denied something they deserve — for no good reason — that is unjust. Equally, if someone escapes blame or gains something they do not deserve — again for no good reason — that is also unjust.

To truly understand "unjust," you need to first feel what "just" means. Justice is the idea that people should get what they deserve — no more, no less — and that everyone should be treated fairly under the same rules. A just outcome is one that is earned, fair, balanced, and morally correct.

"Unjust" is the direct opposite. It describes anything that breaks that balance — where deserving people are treated badly, or undeserving people are treated well, or where rules are applied unfairly.
The Moral Weight of the Word

"Unjust" is not a light word. It carries moral seriousness. When you call something unjust, you are making a strong claim: that something is not merely unlucky or inconvenient, but actually wrong at the level of ethics and fairness.

For example, if it rains on your picnic, that is unfortunate. But it is not unjust, because no one did anything wrong. However, if your employer fires you because of your religion while keeping less-qualified colleagues, that is unjust — because a person with power made a morally wrong decision that harmed you unfairly.

This is important: unjust situations almost always involve human choices, systems, or rules — not accidents of nature. Injustice is done by someone or something.
How It Is Used in Real Life

Unjust can describe many different things.

A law can be unjust. Historically, laws that prevented certain people from voting, owning property, or receiving equal education were called unjust laws — because they denied people basic rights for no morally acceptable reason.

A punishment can be unjust. If a person is sent to prison for a crime they did not commit, or if someone receives an extremely harsh sentence for a very minor offense, the punishment is unjust because it does not match what the person actually deserves.

A decision can be unjust. If a judge, a teacher, a boss, or anyone in authority makes a ruling or judgment that ignores the facts, favors one side without reason, or punishes someone unfairly, that decision is unjust.

A system can be unjust. Entire organizations or social systems can be unjust — for example, a workplace that consistently pays women less than men for the exact same work, without any valid reason, operates unjustly.

Treatment of a person can be unjust. If someone is mocked, excluded, attacked, or denied opportunities simply because of who they are — their race, gender, beliefs, disability — that treatment is unjust.

"Unjust" is often close in meaning to words like unfair, wrong, cruel, and biased, but it is not the same as any of them.

"Unfair" is the closest to "unjust," but "unfair" is softer and more casual. You might say it is unfair that your sibling got a bigger slice of cake. But you would say it is unjust that an innocent person is imprisoned. "Unjust" carries deeper moral seriousness and is used when fundamental rights or principles of fairness have been violated.

"Wrong" is very broad. Many things can be wrong — lying to a friend is wrong, but you would not typically call it unjust. "Unjust" specifically points to violations of fairness and what people deserve.

"Cruel" focuses on causing unnecessary suffering or pain, often out of meanness. Something can be unjust without being cruel (for example, a quietly biased hiring process), and something can be cruel without being unjust in a legal sense.

"Biased" means favoring one side unfairly. A biased decision can lead to an unjust outcome, but bias describes the attitude or leaning, while "unjust" describes the result or the act itself.

"Illegal" means against the law. This is completely different from unjust. Something can be entirely legal but deeply unjust — for example, certain historical laws that were legal but morally wrong. And something can be illegal but not necessarily unjust — like jaywalking.
Something Is Not Unjust Just Because It Feels Bad

This is a subtlety worth understanding. Not every negative outcome is unjust. If you study poorly and fail an exam, the failing grade feels bad, but it is not unjust — it reflects what you actually earned. If a criminal is punished according to fair laws and due process, the punishment may be unpleasant for them but it is not unjust.

"Unjust" specifically requires that fairness or moral rightness has been violated. There must be a genuine mismatch between what someone deserves and what they receive.

"Unjust" can describe both small personal situations and enormous social or historical events. A single teacher unfairly blaming one student is unjust on a small scale. Centuries of slavery were unjust on a massive historical scale. The word works at both levels.

However, because the word carries moral weight, it is generally used for things that matter — situations where a real right or a real person's dignity, freedom, safety, or fair treatment is at stake.

The noun form is "injustice" — meaning the quality or act of being unjust. "He suffered a great injustice." The adverb form is "unjustly" — meaning in an unjust manner. "She was unjustly punished." The antonym (opposite) is "just" — meaning fair, right, and deserved. A just decision is one that gives people exactly what they deserve, under fair and equal rules.

If you had to carry just one idea: something is unjust when it goes against fairness and what people rightfully deserve, especially through the actions of people, systems, or laws that have power over others.
16719: When something or someone is described as unkempt, it means they look messy, untidy, and neglected — as if they haven't been properly cared for or groomed in a while. Think of someone who rolls out of bed, doesn't comb their hair, wears wrinkled clothes, and steps outside. That person looks unkempt.
What makes "unkempt" special — the key nuance

The most important thing to understand is that unkempt is not just about being messy in the moment. It carries a sense of ongoing neglect — that care and maintenance are missing, not just temporarily delayed. It's the difference between a garden that's muddy after a rainstorm (messy, but temporarily) and a garden that hasn't been weeded or trimmed in months (unkempt). The word implies that someone or something has been left to fall into disorder over time.
What can be described as unkempt

The word is used most commonly in three contexts:

People and their appearance: This is the most frequent use. A person who is unkempt looks rough, poorly groomed, and dishevelled. Their hair might be tangled and uncombed, their beard overgrown, their clothes dirty or rumpled. The word describes their overall look of not having taken care of themselves.

Hair specifically: Unkempt hair is perhaps the single most classic usage. It means hair that is tangled, matted, sticking out in different directions, and clearly hasn't been brushed or styled.

Places and outdoor spaces: A garden, yard, lawn, or building can also be unkempt. An unkempt garden is overgrown with weeds, with hedges that haven't been trimmed and grass that hasn't been cut. An unkempt house looks run-down and uncared for.

Unkempt is mildly to moderately negative. It is not a harsh insult, but it clearly suggests that the standard of care or grooming is poor. Describing someone as unkempt in a professional setting (like a job interview) implies they are making a poor impression. In other contexts, like describing a traveller who has been camping for a week, it's more neutral and descriptive than judgmental.

Unkempt has a slightly formal and literary feel to it. In everyday casual conversation, people are more likely to say "messy," "scruffy," or "rough-looking." You'll see unkempt used frequently in written descriptions — in novels, news articles, and formal writing.

Words that are close in meaning to unkempt include: dishevelled, scruffy, untidy, slovenly, bedraggled, rumpled, and tousled (especially for hair). All of these describe a similar lack of neatness, though each has its own shade of meaning. Dishevelled is perhaps the closest synonym.

The opposite of unkempt is neat, tidy, well-groomed, or spruce. Interestingly, the word kempt (meaning well-combed and tidy) actually does exist in English, but it is very rarely used today — unkempt has completely outlived its positive counterpart in everyday use.

• After three days in the wilderness, he emerged looking unkempt — beard overgrown, hair tangled, and clothes stained with mud.
  • The abandoned property sat behind an unkempt yard full of weeds and broken fences.
  • She had clearly rushed out the door; her unkempt hair and wrinkled blouse gave her away.
  • The old professor was brilliant but famously unkempt, never paying much attention to his appearance.
  • Years of neglect had left the once-beautiful garden looking completely unkempt.

Unkempt means looking messy and neglected due to a lack of grooming or care — not just a quick accident, but a noticeable absence of upkeep. If it looks like nobody has bothered to tidy, groom, or maintain it in a while, the word you want is unkempt.
